title: Understanding Color Contrast Through Interactive Examples
excerpt: A hands-on look at WCAG text contrast ratios, with tools for low and high contrast, random 7:1 pairs, and matching a color you want to keep.
author: Johnny Hammond
content:
Interview question: “How do you reason about text color contrast, and what do the WCAG ratios actually guarantee?”

This article answers that question with three tools you can use in the page. I wrote the explanation and rebuilt the examples in React. Earlier versions were separate one-page experiments. Those pages painted the whole document, and the pairing tool could freeze the tab when a color could not reach 7:1. The versions below stay inside a sample, stop when a target is impossible, and leave the rest of the site alone.

What a contrast ratio measures

A contrast ratio compares the relative luminance of two colors. Luminance is a weighted brightness, not the raw red, green, and blue numbers. The ratio runs from 1:1, when the colors are the same, to 21:1, for black and white. A larger ratio means the colors separate more. It does not describe a particular visual impairment, and it does not grade an entire interface.

WCAG uses that ratio for text. The authoritative write-ups are Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.3, Contrast (Minimum) and Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.6, Contrast (Enhanced). Level A does not set a minimum text contrast ratio. The familiar 4.5:1 and 3:1 figures are Level AA. The enhanced 7:1 and 4.5:1 figures are Level AAA.

The numbers you see in these tools are rounded for reading. The pass or fail decision uses the full ratio. A pair that passes one of these text thresholds still does not mean the page is accessible. Contrast says nothing, by itself, about focus, names, keyboard use, motion, or the meaning of color.

Low contrast and high contrast

Low contrast in the first tool means a ratio below 3:1. That is a teaching example of text that is hard to separate. It is not “Level A.” High contrast means 7:1 or higher, the enhanced target for normal-size text. Choose a mode, then press Generate example. The foreground, background, and ratio are written out next to the sample. Only the sample uses the experimental colors, so the controls stay readable.

Try both modes. A low-contrast sample should report a ratio under 3:1. A high-contrast sample should report 7:1 or more. If the rounded number sits on a boundary, the tool shows extra digits so the display does not disagree with the check.

A random pair at 7:1 or higher

The second tool only looks for strong pairs. Press Generate pair and it picks a foreground and a background whose contrast is at least 7:1. It shows both hex values and the ratio. Clicking the article, or anywhere else on the page, does not generate a new pair and does not change the site theme.

Use this when you want a fresh combination and you do not need to keep a brand color. Generate again as many times as you like. Each result stands on its own.

Keep a color you already chose

The third tool starts from your color and finds the other one. Type a hex value or use the picker. They stay on the same color. #RGB and #RRGGBB are both accepted and normalized to six digits. Say whether your color is the foreground or the background. The target starts at AAA normal text, 7:1. You can switch to AA normal text, 4.5:1. Generate matching color keeps the base color exactly and reports the pair, the sample, and the real ratio.

If the hex value is incomplete or not a color, the message under the button tells you what to fix. Change the target or the role and generate again when you want another match. The tool will not swap your base color for a different one.

Why 7:1 is sometimes impossible

Every color has a ceiling. The highest contrast it can reach is the better of its contrast against black and its contrast against white. Mid-luminance colors top out well below 7:1. #777777 is one of them: its best partner is still only about 4.7:1. No search, however long, will find a 7:1 partner, because none exists.

The pairing tool checks that ceiling before it searches. When the target is impossible, it says so and shows the maximum ratio. It leaves both your color and your selected target alone, so you can pick a different color or a lower target yourself. The random generators are also limited to a fixed number of tries, then fall back to a known pair that still meets the requested range.

Normal text and large text

The same ratio means different things for different text sizes. For normal text, AA is 4.5:1 and AAA is 7:1. For large text, AA is 3:1 and AAA is 4.5:1. Large text means at least 18 point regular type, which is 24 CSS pixels, or 14 point bold type, which is about 18.67 CSS pixels. It is not enough to call every large size “about 24px,” because the bold threshold is smaller.

These tools use the normal-text targets, 4.5:1 and 7:1. If you are checking large text, compare the reported ratio with the large-text row instead of assuming the tool’s label still applies. And again, meeting a text ratio is one criterion. It is not a certificate that the page conforms to WCAG.

What I would say in an interview: Text contrast is a luminance ratio, from 1:1 to 21:1. Level A does not define a text minimum. AA is 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text. AAA is 7:1 for normal text and 4.5:1 for large text. Large text is 18pt regular or 14pt bold.

I would check the full ratio, not a rounded display, and I would compare a chosen color with black and white before promising 7:1. Some colors cannot get there. A passing pair is evidence about those two colors only. It does not make the rest of the interface accessible, and it is not a simulation of a visual impairment.
